title: IF GOD WASN’T ASHAMED TO PUT BREASTS, KISSING, SEMEN, MENSTRUATION, DESIRE, AND MARITAL PLEASURE IN SCRIPTURE—WHY ARE WE ASHAMED TO READ IT?
paragraphs: IF GOD WASN’T ASHAMED TO PUT BREASTS, KISSING, SEMEN, MENSTRUATION, DESIRE, AND MARITAL PLEASURE IN SCRIPTURE—WHY ARE WE ASHAMED TO READ IT?

Maybe the problem was never that the Bible talks about the human body too openly. Maybe the problem is that we have spent so long letting pornography, shame, abuse, lust, and religious embarrassment define these words that we have forgotten God spoke about the body first.
There are verses some Christians read loudly.
And there are verses we suddenly read very, very quietly.
We proclaim John 3:16 without hesitation.
We underline Romans 8.
We quote Psalm 23 at funerals.
We put Philippians 4:13 on shirts, coffee mugs, journals, and Facebook posts.
But then we arrive at the Song of Songs.
And suddenly everybody starts clearing their throat.
We meet a woman speaking about kisses.
A husband praising his wife's breasts.
A wife delighting in being desired.
We turn to Leviticus and find Scripture discussing semen and menstruation with an almost startling matter-of-factness.
We find Proverbs telling a husband to rejoice in the wife of his youth and delight in her love.
And some of us instinctively want to close the Bible.
Not because God became inappropriate.
Because somewhere along the way, we became uncomfortable with something God was never embarrassed to acknowledge.
Read that again.
The God who thundered from Sinai is not embarrassed by the human body.
The God who inspired Scripture did not need us to censor Him.

And maybe some of the shame Christians carry today exists precisely because we have allowed the world to talk endlessly about sexuality while the Church has sometimes responded with little more than silence, awkwardness, warnings, or whispers.
So pornography discipled people.
Movies discipled people.
Hookup culture discipled people.
Trauma discipled people.
Locker rooms discipled people.
Social media discipled people.
Secret browser histories discipled people.
And then many Christians walked into marriage carrying desires they did not understand, wounds they never named, expectations shaped by fantasy, and shame they mistakenly thought came from God.
But what if we went back?
Not back to culture.
Back to Scripture.
Back before pornography stole desire.
Back before lust distorted intimacy.
Back before abuse weaponized vulnerability.
Back before shame convinced people that their bodies were inherently filthy.
Back to the God who created humanity male and female and looked upon His creation and called it “very good” (Genesis 1:27, 31).
Because the Bible does not begin with embarrassed bodies.
It begins with naked people who had no shame.
Genesis 2:25 says the man and his wife were both naked, “and were not ashamed.”
Then sin entered.
And what appeared almost immediately?
Hiding.
Covering.
Fear.
“I was afraid, because I was naked; and I hid myself” (Genesis 3:10).
Do you see the tragedy?
God created the body.
Sin introduced shame.
And ever since Eden, humanity has been confusing the two.
Some people worship the body.
Others despise it.
Some exploit it.
Others pretend it barely exists.
The Gospel does neither.
Christianity does not teach that matter is evil and spirituality means escaping physical existence. At the center of Christianity stands one of the most astonishing declarations imaginable:
The Word became flesh.
Jesus Christ did not rescue humanity by refusing embodiment.
He entered it.
He was conceived.
Born.
Held.
Hungry.
Thirsty.
Tired.
Touched.
Wounded.
Crucified in a real human body.
Raised bodily from the dead.
The Christian story is not God saying the body does not matter.
It is God entering His creation to redeem fallen human beings completely.
Which makes our embarrassment about some biblical language worth examining.
Open Song of Songs 1:2 and the Hebrew does not blush:
יִשָּׁקֵנִי מִנְּשִׁיקוֹת פִּיהוּ
Yishaqeni minneshiqot pihu.
Literally, the woman longs for the kisses of her beloved's mouth.
The Hebrew verb is not secretly describing a committee meeting.
It means kissing.
The text itself speaks openly of kisses and love.
And notice something Christians sometimes miss.
The woman speaks.
She desires.
She expresses affection.
She is not presented merely as an object being desired by a man.
Her voice fills the poem.
Later she says:
אֲנִי לְדוֹדִי וְעָלַי תְּשׁוּקָתוֹ
Ani ledodi, ve'alai teshuqato.
“I am my beloved's, and his desire is for me.”
That word תְּשׁוּקָה — teshuqah carries the idea of desire or longing.
She knows she is desired.
And within the poetry of Song of Songs, that knowledge is not presented as inherently dirty.
Then there are the breasts.
Yes.
Breasts.
Not a modern addition.
Not something inserted by a corrupt translator.
The Hebrew word שַׁד — shad, with the dual form שָׁדַיִם — shadayim, means breasts. It appears repeatedly in Scripture, including several times in Song of Songs.
Song of Songs speaks poetically and appreciatively about the beloved's body.
Why?
Because biblical holiness is not the denial that bodies exist.
Holiness is the ordering of the whole person under God.
That distinction changes everything.
Pornography says, “Consume this body.”
Lust says, “Use this person in your imagination.”
Abuse says, “Your boundaries do not matter.”
Promiscuity says, “Covenant does not matter.”
Shame says, “Your body itself is disgusting.”
But biblical marital love says something profoundly different:
“You are not a product.
You are not pornography.
You are not an object.
You are a person bearing God's image, worthy of dignity, fidelity, tenderness, honor, and covenant love.”
Scripture can celebrate marital affection without endorsing lust because desire and lust are not identical things.
Sin did not invent attraction.
Sin corrupts God's gifts.
Food is good; gluttony corrupts appetite.
Money can serve good purposes; greed corrupts stewardship.
Authority can protect; domination corrupts authority.
Sexuality belongs to God's created order; sexual sin distorts it.
And perhaps that is why Satan gains so much ground whenever Christians decide the answer to sexual corruption is simply never to speak honestly about sexuality.
Silence does not create innocence.
Sometimes silence simply leaves someone else holding the microphone.
Then we reach Leviticus.
Surely, we imagine, the Bible will become vague there.
It does not.
Leviticus 15:16 contains the Hebrew expression:
שִׁכְבַת־זָרַע — shikhvat-zera
The verse refers directly to an emission of semen. The Hebrew זֶרַע — zera means “seed,” and in this bodily context the phrase refers to semen.
Later in the same chapter, Scripture addresses a woman's menstrual discharge. The Hebrew text uses נִדָּה — niddah in this ritual-purity context.
God put these realities into Israel's law.
Without pornography.
Without crude entertainment.
Without giggling.
Without pretending biology does not exist.
That distinction matters enormously.
Leviticus 15 is not an erotic passage. It concerns ritual purity under the Mosaic covenant.
And “unclean” in these passages must not carelessly be turned into “morally sinful.”
Those categories are not automatically identical.
That matters because generations of people—especially women—have sometimes absorbed the idea that ordinary bodily processes make them personally disgusting before God.
The text does not give us permission to make that leap.
The chapter addresses ritual states and purification within Israel's covenantal worship system.
Men are addressed.
Women are addressed.
Bodily discharges are addressed.
Human biology is treated seriously.
There is no need to sanitize the passage, and there is certainly no need to weaponize it against someone's dignity.
Then consider Proverbs 5.
The chapter warns a man intensely against adultery.
And what is God's answer to forbidden sexual desire?
It is not, “Become incapable of desire.”
It redirects desire toward covenant faithfulness.
“Rejoice with the wife of thy youth” (Proverbs 5:18).
Then Scripture describes marital delight in language so intimate that many believers have probably raced through the verses hoping nobody asks them to explain them.
But perhaps we should stop racing.
Because God is teaching something.
Faithfulness is not merely avoiding somebody else's bed.
Marriage is supposed to contain delight.
Tenderness.
Exclusive affection.
Joy.
Desire that has learned covenant instead of consumption.
This is important because there are Christians who know exactly what God says “no” to but have never discovered the beauty behind God's “yes.”
No adultery.
No pornography.
No fornication.
No exploitation.
No lustful consumption of another person.
Yes.
Those boundaries matter.
Jesus Himself takes sexual sin so seriously that He confronts lust at the level of the heart in Matthew 5:27–28.
But if our theology stops with prohibition, we have not told the whole biblical story.
God does not merely redeem people from something.
He redeems us for something.
For holiness.
For faithfulness.
For love.
For self-control.
For covenant.
For the ability to see another human being as an image-bearer rather than an object for consumption.
And this is where some people reading this may feel something painful rising.
Because not everybody hears the word “sexuality” and thinks of marriage.
Some remember what happened to them.
Something stolen.
Something watched.
Something done.
Something they did.
Something they cannot erase from their memory.
A bedroom.
A screen.
A relationship.
An abortion.
An affair.
A secret.
An addiction.
A violation.
A betrayal.
A night you desperately wish you could remove from history.
Maybe you have spent years believing that if Christians really knew everything about you, they would never look at you the same way again.
Maybe you believe Jesus looks at you that way too.
Listen carefully.
The Gospel does not say sin is imaginary.
It says grace is greater.
Jesus never needed to rename darkness “light” in order to forgive sinners.
At the cross, sin is taken so seriously that Christ dies.
And sinners are loved so deeply that Christ dies for them.
That is Christianity.
Not denial.
Not humiliation.
Redemption.
Remember the woman in John 8 who was dragged into public shame after being caught in adultery.
People stood around her carrying stones.
Jesus did not call adultery holy.
Neither did He surrender the woman to her accusers.
After the accusers departed, His words held grace and transformation together:
“Neither do I condemn thee: go, and sin no more.”
Grace did not say, “Nothing happened.”
Grace said, in effect, “What happened will not have the final word.”
That is the Gospel Warrior message.
Maybe your story contains a chapter you would never voluntarily read aloud.
Jesus is not frightened by the chapter.
Maybe your sexuality has been distorted by pornography.
Jesus can redeem what lust discipled.
Maybe adultery shattered your marriage.
Repentance cannot make betrayal nonexistent, but Christ can create something beyond the ruins that sin produced.
Maybe somebody violated you.
Their sin does not determine your worth.
Maybe you crossed boundaries you knew were wrong and now conviction is crushing you.
Do not confuse conviction with a sentence of hopelessness.
Conviction says, “Come into the light.”
Condemnation whispers, “Hide forever.”
The Gospel says:
Come.
Confess.
Repent.
Believe.
Receive mercy.
Walk differently.
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness” (1 John 1:9).
That verse is for sexual sin too.
The blood of Jesus does not mysteriously lose its power when the sin becomes embarrassing.
Think about that.
We sing that His blood washes sin.
Then someone confesses pornography and we act as though we discovered an exception.
Someone confesses adultery and we wonder whether grace has enough oxygen to reach that far.
Someone admits years of secret sexual sin and believes their testimony is permanently destroyed.
But Peter denied Christ.
Paul persecuted Christians.
David's history contained devastating sexual sin and bloodshed.
The Samaritan woman carried a complicated relational history.
The Corinthian church included people rescued from serious sexual immorality, and Paul told them:
“And such were some of you.”
Were.
Then:
“But ye are washed, but ye are sanctified, but ye are justified in the name of the Lord Jesus” (1 Corinthians 6:11).
Do not miss the miracle hidden inside that grammar.
Your past can be true without being your master.
Your sin can be real without becoming your identity.
Your wounds can be real without becoming your destiny.
Your body can have memories while your soul learns freedom.
You can repent without pretending.
You can heal without rewriting history.
Because Jesus does something infinitely better than pretending the scandal never happened.
He writes grace into the story after it.
This is why Christians must recover the courage to talk biblically about bodies.
Our children need something better than embarrassment.
Teenagers need something stronger than “don't.”
Singles need theology that honors holiness without treating unmarried people as incomplete human beings.
Married couples need permission to understand that covenant affection is not spiritually inferior to prayer, worship, service, or Bible reading simply because it involves the body.
People trapped in pornography need more than shame.
People wounded by sexual abuse need compassion without blame.
People living in sexual sin need truth without hatred.
And everybody needs Jesus.
Because sexual brokenness is not solved merely by becoming more sexually informed.
We need regenerated hearts.
We need the Holy Spirit.
We need repentance.
We need grace.
We need a Savior.
Christian sexual ethics are not ultimately about pretending desire does not exist.
They are about surrendering desire to Christ.
Jesus does not merely ask for your church attendance.
He claims your eyes.
Your imagination.
Your browser history.
Your relationships.
Your private messages.
Your fantasies.
Your body.
Your future marriage.
Your present singleness.
Your wounds.
Your desires.
Your secrets.
All of you.
Paul writes:
There it is.
Not despise your body.
Not worship your body.
Not sell your body.
Not use somebody else's body.
Glorify God in your body.
The Gospel is neither prudish nor pornographic.
It is holy.
And holiness is far more beautiful than either extreme.
So perhaps the question is not:
“Why does the Bible talk about breasts, kisses, semen, menstruation, desire, and marital pleasure?”
Perhaps the more revealing question is:
Why did we ever think God needed our embarrassment to protect His holiness?
God does not need censorship.
He requires faithful interpretation.
Song of Songs is poetry, so read it as poetry.
Leviticus is covenantal law, so read it in its covenantal and ritual context.
Proverbs is wisdom literature, so hear its wisdom.
Jesus' teaching exposes the heart, so let it expose yours.
Paul's teaching on the body calls Christians toward holiness, so surrender your body to Christ.
Context protects us from turning Scripture into either pornography or prudishness.
And Christ stands at the center of the whole Christian story.
Creation tells us the body is God's workmanship.
The Fall explains why desire becomes distorted and shame enters human experience.
The Law demonstrates that God speaks seriously about embodied human life.
Wisdom celebrates faithful covenant love.
The prophets expose spiritual and physical unfaithfulness.
Jesus enters human flesh.
The cross purchases sinners.
The resurrection declares that embodied existence matters.
The Holy Spirit makes believers temples.
And the promised resurrection tells Christians that God is not ultimately throwing His creation away.
He is making all things new.
Maybe this article made you uncomfortable.
Good questions sometimes begin there.
Not because discomfort proves something is true.
But because discomfort can reveal assumptions we have never examined.
So examine them with Scripture open.
If this exposed shame you have been carrying, you do not have to describe your private history publicly.

And if you have already watched Christ redeem an area of your life you once thought could never be restored, tell somebody what His grace has done. Your testimony may become the sentence another wounded person desperately needed to read tonight.
Not because an algorithm is sacred.
Because somebody you know may be silently drowning in shame while appearing perfectly fine at church.
Send this privately to the person you know is fighting pornography.
Send it to the Christian who has confused holiness with embarrassment.
Send it to the wounded person who needs to hear that what was done to them does not erase their God-given dignity.
Because sooner or later somebody will tell you Christianity teaches that the human body is inherently dirty, and you may need to return to the Scriptures and remember what they actually say.
And stay close to Gospel Warrior if you want daily Scripture, conviction, encouragement, biblical truth, healing, discipleship, and spiritual nourishment centered on Jesus Christ.
It does not.
Not because giving earns salvation.
It cannot.
It doesn't.
Scripture does not give us authority to make those claims.

What Scripture does teach is that Gospel ministry may legitimately receive material support. Paul writes that “the Lord ordained that they which preach the gospel should live of the gospel” (1 Corinthians 9:14).
Scripture also guards the giver from spiritual manipulation:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart… not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.” (2 Corinthians 9:7)
The Greek is striking:
μὴ ἐκ λύπης ἢ ἐξ ἀνάγκης
mē ek lypēs ē ex anankēs—
not from grief or reluctance, and not from ἀνάγκη — anankē, necessity, constraint, or compulsion.
That means biblical generosity should never need spiritual blackmail.
And sometimes support costs nothing at all.
One share may place the Gospel in front of someone we could never reach ourselves.
One tag may find somebody on the night they were preparing to give up.
One comment may tell another struggling Christian, “You are not fighting alone.”
But the deepest reason to support Gospel work should never be merchandise.
It should be mission.
Give freely.
Share intentionally.
Tag personally.
Save what strengthens you.
Follow so you can keep growing with us.
But above everything else—
Follow Jesus.
Because Gospel Warrior cannot save you.
A church cannot bleed for you.
A Christian product cannot cleanse your conscience.
Only Jesus Christ was crucified for sinners.
Only Jesus rose from the grave.
Only Jesus can take the parts of your story you are terrified to uncover and bring them beneath the authority of His truth and the mercy of His cross.
Maybe that is what you needed to hear tonight.
God already knows about the body.
He already knows about the desire.
He already knows about the addiction.
He already knows what happened behind that door.
He already knows what appeared on that screen.
He already knows what somebody did to you.
He already knows what you did.
He already knows what you regret.
He already knows what you have been hiding.
And still the Gospel invitation stands:
Come into the light.
Repent where you have sinned.
Receive grace where you have been forgiven.
Seek healing where you have been wounded.
Learn holiness where desire has been distorted.
Stop calling God's creation dirty.
Stop calling sin harmless.
Stop calling shame repentance.
And stop believing your darkest chapter is powerful enough to steal the pen from Jesus.
The scandal may explain how you arrived here—but grace can determine where your story goes next.
